A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed a physically realistic model of scattering radiative transport in frozen hydrometeor particles that has been tested and shown to work in all-sky situations, in all frequencies from 10 to 183 GHz, and in all weather regimes globally.

the scattering properties of snow are now well understood and can be accurately simulated in all-sky situations, allowing the use of microwave observations for all weather situations and all frequencies.
the scattering radiative transfer is improved and that this is sufficient to allow assimilation of all-sky microwave data in NWP models.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the choice of particle shape for radiative transfer is important.
the discrete dipole method is a very useful tool for computing scattering properties of ice hydrometeoers.
scattering radiative transfer is not a "black box" and that, if we are to use passive microwave data for NWP, it needs to be as accurate as possible.
